subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO SETTING UP OF EMPLOYER-EMPLOYEE COUNCIL

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO SETTING UP OF EMPLOYER-EMPLOYEE COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make an announcement which I think will be of interest to hon. members.
In conformity with the government's announced policy of promoting employee representation in private industry and the improvement of industrial relations generally, the treasury board has decided to provide for the setting up of an employer-employee council in the public service of Canada. In working out this policy the treasury board will accept as its general model, with the necessary adaptations to suit Canadian conditions, the pattern which has been evolved in the L'nited Kingdom through the application of so-called Whitley councils to the British public service. The board is therefore providing immediately for the establishment of a national joint council of the public service of Canada equally representative of the official and staff sides of the public service, but, as it is desirable that the new organization and procedure should evolve as a result of consultation and general discussion rather than being imposed from above in any cut and dried fashion, we are immediately suggesting a tentative constitution of the new joint council and wish to have the council itself give the fullest consideration to all questions relating to its permanent organization and procedure and to make recommendations for a permanent constitution to the treasury board within a specified period.
Initially, the national joint council is to consist of six representatives of the official or employer side of the public service, and six representatives of the staff or employee side. The Civil Service Federation, the Civil Service Association, the Amalgamated Civil Servants, the Professional Institute, and the Dominion Customs and Excise Officers' Association are each being asked to name one representative to the council, and the three organizations which represent the postal employees are being asked to select one representative to

Public Service-Council
represent them. The treasury board will itself nominate six senior civil servants to act as the representatives of the government, included amongst whom will be a representative of the Civil Service Commission.
The national joint council will act in an advisory capacity to the treasury board in all matters affecting the conditions of work in the public service. In certain fields their recommendations may appropriately be made directly to the Civil Service Commission. The council will, of course, not have any executive powers which would impair the responsibility of the cabinet or treasury board or Civil Service Commission, or possibly infringe upon the authority of parliament. While the council's functions will therefore be advisory only, it is clear that if both sides take their responsibilities seriously and endeavour to make the new organization a means of promoting better understanding, improved morale and greater efficiency in the civil service, any recommendations of the council reached by agreement should carry great weight with the treasury board and the Civil Service Commission.
The general purpose of the national joint council will be to secure a greater measure of cooperation between the state in its capacity of employer and the general body of civil servants in matters affecting the civil service, with a view to increased efficiency in the public service combined with the well-being of those employed; to provide machinery for dealing with grievances and for making suggestions for improved efficiency; and generally to bring together the experience and different points of view of representatives of the administrative, clerical and manipulative sides of the civil service.
More specifically, the duties of the national council will be:
(a)	to recommend to the treasury board the best means for securing to the staff a greater share in and greater responsibility for the determination and observance of the conditions under which their duties are carried out, and in particular to consider and report to the treasury board not later than June 30, 1944, on a permanent constitution for the national joint council of the public service of Canada, on the advisability of providing for the establishment of various departmental or district joint councils, and, if such are recommended, on the organization and procedure of such joint councils and their relationship to the national joint council;
(b)	to make recommendations to the treasury board or the Civil Service Commission, as the case may require, regarding the
100-50J	,
general principles governing conditions of service in the public service of Canada, including recruitment, training, hours of work, promotions, discipline, tenure, remuneration and superannuation;
(c)	to recommend to the treasury board or the Civil Service Commission, or both, the best means for utilizing the ideas and experience of the staff;
(d)	to make recommendations to the Civil Service Commission regarding the encouragement of the further education of civil servants and their training in higher administration and organization;
(e) to make	recommendations to the treasury board or the Civil Service Commission, or both, regarding the improvement of office procedures and organization and the provision of opportunities for the full consideration of suggestions by the staff on this subject; and
(f) to make recommendations	to the treasury board regarding proposed legislation in so far as it has a bearing upon the position of civil servants in relation to their employment.
In the tentative constitution which is being provided for the national joint council, provision is being made for the holding of regular and special meetings, for the appointment of a chairman (who shall be a representative of the treasury board) and a vice-chairman (who shall be a representative of the staff side and chosen by the staff representatives), for the filling of vacancies, and for other procedural and organizational matters.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY FOR COMING MILK YEAR
speechtext:
I desire to make an announcement of government policy on milk and other dairy products covering the milk year which begins May 1, 1944. and continues until April 30, 1945.
I should like at the outset of my remarks to record the appreciation of the government of the splendid job which the dairy producers of Canada have done and are continuing to do on production in spite of difficulties. The season of 1942-43 was unusually favourable and a record production was secured. The latter half of the season of 1943-44 has been very unfavourable and milk producers have done a remarkably good job in maintaining milk production at high levels.
The chief difficulty beginning in November was related to a short supply of feed in eastern Canada, resulting from the poorest crop which

Dairy Products-Government Policy
eastern Canada has harvested in fifty years. Realizing the danger of a drop in supplies the government increased the subsidies on all dairy products between October 1,1943, and April 30, 1944. This, together with assistance given toward the movement of feed grain from the West, has resulted in fair supplies under extremely difficult circumstances.
It is hoped that weather conditions will be more favourable throughout 1944, although it is recognized that to the extent that grain feed is required an improvement in the position cannot come until a new crop is harvested in the
east. By far the greater part of dairy production will, however, depend upon pastures during the early part of the season, and to that extent costs will be reduced as compared with the winter season.
The new subsidy levels are therefore placed on a lower plane in the first five months than they were during the last seven months of the preceding year, but on most items will be placed at the same level for the last seven months.

We are at present negotiating a contract with Great Britain for cheese, which we hope will provide for Britian to take all the cheese we can provide during the next two years. Any surpluses of butter or canned milk which may result can be marketed in Britain.
We think these subsidies, along with the door under prices already provided through our agreements and otherwise for dairy products, should-result, if weather is favourable, in a record production in dairy products in 1944.

speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 6, to amend the railway act.

subtopic: FREE RAILWAY TRANSPORTATION FOR MEMBERS OF HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: FREE RAILWAY TRANSPORTATION FOR MEMBERS OF HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
This bill proposes to amend the Railway Act in order to provide certain concessions in railway fares to our soldiers during this war. At the present time the Railway Act does not provide any special concessions for soldiers; it applies only to civilians. The board of transport commissioners has no power to order any special rates for soldiers. During the last war soldiers were carried for half fare during week-ends and during this war they are carried for half fare on all days. However, the camps are located all across Canada and there should be some body such as the transport commission which should have power over it, to see that fares are reasonable, grant any necessary concessions, and eliminate any discrimination against our soldiers.

subtopic: PROFITS ON WAR CONTRACTS
speechtext:
1.	In no case has it been necessary to exercise the powers given under subsection 4 of section 13 of the Department of Munitions and Supply Act. It has been found preferable to enter renegotiation proceedings on a less formal basis and in all cases in which the negotiations have been completed, a satisfactory price adjustment has been made on an amicable basis. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR DEPARTMENT-GEORGE HODGE-P.C. 9384
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	Mr. Hodge was a member of an industrial disputes inquiry commission which was appointed in June, 1941. Mr. Hodge has not functioned on this board since the national war labour board was established in November, 1941.
In November, 1941, at the request of the then Minister of Labour, Hon. N. A. McLarty, the Canadian Pacific Railway made Mr. Hodge available, without salary, to act as a member of the national war labour board. He subsequently became a member of the executive committee of three.
Since the national war labour board was reconstituted in February, 1943, Mr. Hodge has served as a technical adviser to the board, a full-time post; as a member of the national war labour committee, and as a member of the national selective service advisory board.
Mr. Hodge was a member of the former national labour supply council. As such Mr. Hodge was not technically in the employ of the Department of Labour.
3.	Mr. Hodge has at no time received any salary from the Department of Labour. He has been paid only actual expenses incurred by him as undemoted:
Number of days: fiscal year 1941-42, 142; fiscal year 1942-43, 362; fiscal year 1943-44 (to January 31, 1944), 304; total, 808.

It should be noted that fees paid to Mr. Hodge as a member of the industrial disputes inquiry commission under order in council P.C. 4020 are not included in the above figures. These amounted to: remuneration at $20 per day, 1941-42, $1,440; actual travelling expenses, 1941-42, $707.27.

Questions

In respect to the national war labour board, Mr. Hodge fulfilled the normal functions of an executive officer while a member of the executive committee. He now serves as a technical adviser to the board and is a member of the national war labour committee.
As a member of the national selective service advisory board, Mr. Hodge participates with other members in matters affecting national selective service.
5.	See answers to questions 1 and 2.

subtopic: POST-WAR AVIATION CONFERENCE
speechtext:
1.	The government knows of no proposal to hold a conference on post-war international aviation matters in the United States in the near future. subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PROCEDURE IN ISSUING CALL-UP NOTICES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PROCEDURE IN ISSUING CALL-UP NOTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 7, as will be noted on page 205 of Hansard, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) brought up the case of a soldier who had been in the army since 1942 but recently received a call-up notice under the National Resources Mobilization Act.
I have made inquiries about this case and I find that the master registration card of the man in question shows that on registering he gave the date of his birth as July IS, 1925. It has been ascertained that he enlisted on March 30, 1942, at Petawawa, stating at that time that he was bom on November 22, 1923. Consequently, at the time of enlistment he was under seventeen years of age.
Registration cards in the divisional registrars' offices are kept in order of the year of birth and the registrar would not be in a position to prevent the issuance of a call-up notice to a man reaching the age of eighteen and a half years against a notice of enlistment from the armed forces giving a birth date that would make the callee twenty years of age. It will be realized that this difference in ages would cause considerable confusion as to identification. The recent call-up of this man went out because he had reached the age of eighteen and a half years based on his registration record.
I might add that in November, 1942, a change was made in the method by which the armed forces advise this department of enlistments, and under the present system the registrar receives copy of a pro-forma for each man enlisted through very definite channels.
While there is always the possibility of clerical error there would be relatively few cases under the present system whereby a man already enlisted would receive a call-up under mobilization regulations, unless, of course, the information provided by the man at the time of enlistment was contrary to information given at the time of registration.
I return to the hon. gentleman the documents he gave me, with the exception of the railway ticket and warrants for meals, which will not be required.

speechtext:
Is the Minister of Labour aware that some employers, particularly in the province of Ontario, in industries where a vote has already been taken to determine the bargaining agency, and where negotiations with the bargaining agency so determined were entered 
into, are refusing, since the tabling of the wartime labour relations regulations order, P.C. 1003, to continue negotiations on the pretext that they are not clear what the status of the bargaining agency previously determined will be under the new order? Is the minister in a position to make a statement that would clarify the order as it relates to the situation I have described?

subtopic: WARTIME LABOUR RELATIONS REGULATIONS, P.C. 1003
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question of the hon. member for Vancouver East, I should like to make a statement regarding the application of the wartime labour relations regulations, P.C. 1003, particularly in those provinces where legislation is at present in force providing for certification of bargaining representatives before collective bargaining is commenced. The provinces of Ontario and British Columbia have such legislation. So has Quebec, although I am under the impression that machinery has not yet been completed to administer the labour relations act recently passed by the Quebec legislature.
Hon. members will be aware that the wartime labour relations regulations, approved by the governor in council on February 17, are not yet in force. Section 48 provides for their coming into force on a day to be fixed by the governor in council. We first must set up the wartime labour relations board and the machinery to carry out the regulations. However, I can assure the house there will not be unnecessary delay in doing so.
In those provinces where machinery exists for the certification of bargaining representatives, and pending the coming into force of the new federal regulations, I would say that employees and employers should observe the terms of the existing provincial legislation and bargain in good faith after the bargaining representatives have been certified. If as a result of this bargaining a collective agreement is consummated before our regulations come into force, the collective agreement should be regarded as a valid one. If on the other hand the negotiations following the certification of bargaining representatives under provincial laws fail to produce a satisfactoiy agreement, either party may make application to the Minister of Labour for the establishment of a board of conciliation and investigation under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, provided the industry is one coming within the scope of that act as extended by order in council P.C. 3495.
It should be noted that the suspension of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act occurs only when the wartime labour relations regulations come into force. In other cases provincial legislation may provide for

War Appropriation-Army
further reference to the competent authority when agreement on the terms of a collective agreement cannot be reached.
Where certified bargaining representatives are in negotiation with employers when our federal wartime labour relations regulations come into force, there might be some apprehension that certification of such bargaining representatives will again have to be sought.
Section 36 (2) of our regulations empowers the Minister of Labour, with the approval of the governor in council, to enter into agreements with the governments of the provinces to provide for the administration, within those provinces, of the regulations. I would say that when the terms of these agreements are under consideration by the provinces and ourselves all questions which may arise, such as that of the recognition by the board of the decision of the labour court of Ontario or other provincial authorities with regard to certification of bargaining agencies or representatives, will be fully considered and adequately covered.
I make this statement at this time because I realize that some uncertainty is bound to exist in the minds of trade union officers and officials of employing companies, engaged in proceedings initiated under provincial regulations, as to their status under the national regulations; uncertainty which might tend to delay the current negotiations until our regulations are effective.
The interests of industrial peace and of the war effort will best be served if parties to negotiations now in progress continue their negotiations with a genuine desire to reach a satisfactory outcome.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, despite the statement of the minister concerning the matter of the amount of allowances payable to mothers of men in the armed services, I should like to press him to give the matter further consideration. It seemed to me that there was an inconsistency between the statement which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) made on page 613 of Hansard and that which he made on page 619. On page 613, when he was discussing the reasons for cutting off the allowances of dependents to any soldier who is absent without leave, he made this statement:
Dependents' allowance is not granted as compensation to a wife because she has lost the comfort of or association with her husband. It is paid to the wife in order to promote the well-being of the service, and to relieve the anxiety which husbands overseas would have, if such payment were not being made.
In passing, I do not agree altogether with the spirit of that statement. It seems to me that dependents deserve some consideration in their own own right rather than simply on behalf of the men in the forces. But even taking the statement at its face value, I emphasize these words of the minister:
It is paid to the wife in order to promote the well-being of the service, and to relieve the anxiety which husbands overseas would have, if such payment were not being made.
War Appropriation-Army

On pages 619 and 620, when we were discussing the difference between amounts allowed to wives and to mothers of soldiers, the minister pointed out that in the case of a wife, the $35 is given to her as of right, whether she has nothing or is a millionaire; and then he went on to say that the mother received the $25, not necessarily the whole of that amount, only if dependency could be established. There is also the further regulation that her total income outside assigned pay must not exceed $65. As all hon. members know, there are many men in the forces who have a deep anxiety because of the economic position of the mother at home, and if the minister is going to take the position which is set out on page 613 in regard to the morale of men in the services, I submit it ought to apply to mothers of men in the forces. If it is desirable for the morale of the forces to pay $35 to wives, it is at least equally desirable that the maximum payable to mothers should be raised to that figure, $35.
I hope that the minister and the government will give this matter further consideration, because it affects a great many men in the forces. Many a young man is just as much concerned about the economic circumstances of his mother, particularly where there is invalidity on the part of the father, as married men are for their wives and families. At the same time I should like to press further this point with regard to the regulation that sets $65 as the ceiling on income for mothers in this class. It has the effect of discouraging mothers who might otherwise get some kind of work as a means of stepping up their income, because when they do they are cut down in the amount of the allowance they receive. It should be remembered that in hundreds, perhaps thousands, of cases the mother is called upon to put up with conditions inferior to those under which she lived when the son was at home working and contributing to the upkeep of the home.
I bring to the attention of the minister and of the government these two points-the desirability of increasing to $35 the maximum allowance paid to mothers, and of raising the $65 ceiling to, I would say, $75, or better still, $100.

I support the very reasonable plea made by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). If a soldier can establish the fact that he was contributing to the support of his parents prior to his enlistment, I submit that automatically one of the parents ought to be entitled to dependents' allowance^ Let me give an instance I came across the other day of a

w'idow on a farm who had her youngest son helping her to operate it. The boy joined the army. The mother cannot possibly continue working the farm without men to help her, and at the present time she cannot hire reliable farm help. She therefore leaves the farm and goes to teach school, though she is not by any means a young woman. This boy had been contributing toward her support during all the years he was working on the farm. Now, because his mother is teaching school, she is not allowed the dependent's allowance. He can assign part of his pay as a contribution, but she cannot get dependent's allowance. If she stayed in town and sat around, she would get it, but because she teaches in a small country school, where teachers are hard to get, and receives $75 a month, she cannot get the dependent's allowance, since her income is in excess of $65 even without the dependent's allowance.
As the regulation stands at the present time, this woman could not get the full dependent's allowance if her income were more than $40. Her total income' could not be more than $65. The government have set a very low figure if they think that the mother of a man in the services can live on $65 a month. It is far too low. This boy has been contributing for years to his mother's support; now he dons the king's uniform, and I suggest the government should underwite that boy's responsibility and shoulder the provision for the dependency of his mother, which the boy has been doing throughout the years. I ask the minister to consider the matter further.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, I have been thinking that when they return to Canada they should be put with other men who have served in active warfare. The case I have in mind is that of a young man who, upon returning from overseas was sent to a barracks. Having been there only a few days he found he could not stick it any longer. Apparently his nerves were wrought up, with the result that he went away AW.L. That young man came to see me, and I said to him, "Why are you here in uniform?" He said, "I am away without leave." Then I said to him, "My dear boy, I think you ought to go right back to barracks and report." He replied, "I am now away four days." I pointed out to him that that did not make any difference, that he could not take the law into his own hands, and urged that he report back to his superior officer. The young man did go back, and he was put into the clink for four days. When he got out his nerves again got the better of him, and he went away for a period of sixty-five days, returning to his home in Toronto. Apparently no effort was made to find him. After he had been away those sixty-five days he went back to barracks, and told me that when he returned to barracks his name was written off the rolls. I had suggested to him that he go back and tell his full story. This time he was put into the clink for twenty-eight days.
After that detention-and I shall not say whether it was inflicted rightly or wrongly; I do not know, and I have no fault to findr- he went away again, and stayed away without leave for a further number of days. Upon his return he was put into the . clink for another twenty-eight days. Upon his release he went away again. When I was home I went to see him in barracks, because he had written me a letter. I said to him, "You should not do this. When you get out you ought to act fairly with the officials." "Well," he said, "I cannot stick it; my nerves are so shot that I cannot do otherwise." Then he showed me wounds on his hands, another on the side of his head, and he told me that he had suffered a third, and pointed out that
he could not stand it. I told him I was going to report his case to the officials, and that has been done.
I have mentioned the matter because I have felt that there might be other cases of a similar kind. I do not wish to give this man's name or barracks, but I should like tile minister to look into the matter as presented in my letter and see what can be done when he comes out again on or about March 4 after a total of 128 days' detention. I am only a layman, but I was convinced that his nerves were in bad condition. I have no fault to find with the treatment he has received from the officials. But if this is a condition which applies to other soldiers returning from actual warfare, they should be placed in separate camps and ought not to be in close association with the young men who are coming in, particularly in view of the fact that they do not seem to get along well when they are placed together.

May I return to the matter of mothers' allowances, and ask two questions of the minister? First, do I understand if the $25 allowance is not sufficient to cover a mother's needs, in the event of her having smaller children dependent upon her, there is a provision under which more than S25 can be paid? My second question is this: Will the minister undertake to reconsider the ceiling price placed upon earnings? This is working an unfairness. The effect is that no mother can take a full-time job, paying $10 a week or more, without losing part of the $25 allowance. There are no full-time jobs for women to-day for which less than $10 a week is offered, although in depression days one might have found that

condition. The result is that if a mother works at all she must forfeit a part of her $25 allowance. She will see others who work only two or three days a week but who receive the full $25. speechtext:
If the mother is earning
money and wants to work five days a week- God bless her if she does-and if the principle is based upon need, then the basic condition for dependents' allowance in respect of mothers does not arise-or, at least, it is reduced to the extent that she is earning from other sources. The anxiety of the son is not there, because he knows his mother is being provided for. He knows, in other words, that she is looking after herself, and that the country is making up the difference, to the total of $65, plus assigned pay.
My hon. friend asks me to reconsider this matter. He makes his request of one who is most sympathetic to the mothers of these men. All I can say to him, however, as I have said to the committee before-and it does not mean anything more than I am saying-is that the position of these mothers is always under consideration. When I say it does not mean more than what I am saying, I mean just that; if there are cases or situations which really justify intervention, then we endeavour to intervene.
I should like the committee, if it will, to remember that what we are endeavouring to do is to take the place of the sons with regard to mothers' earnings. The hon. member for Wey-burn referred to a mother, a daughter and a son on the farm, and pointed out that the son had been contributing to his mother's support for many years. I was going to ask him, not to give me the name in question, but to tell me how much a month the son had contributed through the years, and how much the mother was getting for teaching in the school instead of doing the work she did on the farm. It looked to me as if she must have been getting $25 a month dependents' allowance and at least $40 a month additional from the school. In fact I take it she was getting more than that,

because my hon. friend said that she could not get any dependent's allowance at all, having taken a position at the school. She must have been getting at least $65 at the school, and then she was getting her son's assigned pay, whatever that was. I wondered if she was not better off financially under the circumstances than she had been, having regard to the amounts which the boy had been contributing when they were on the farm. We must remember that the country is taking the place of the boy so far as supporting the mother is concerned, but only up to limits which are considered reasonable. However, the dependents' board of trustees is able in meritorious cases to step in and to provide a supplementary grant to that given by the dependents' allowance board.

I believe I have a still more to the point case than any suggested so far. A man is receiving an old age pension of $25 a month, and his son assigns so much pay to the mother. Both the father and mother are totally incapacitated and are unable to earn any money. Their only income is their old age pension and the assigned pay. The mother is entitled to have an income up to $40 a month, but because her husband is receiving an old age pension he cannot receive a dependent's allowance. There is conflict between the old age pension authorities and the dependents' allowance board. The old age pension regulations provide that if a man has an income, or if there is an income in the family, the old age pension is reduced proportionately. I ask the minister to take up this matter and see if some agreement cannot be reached between the dependents' allowance board and the old age pension authorities in the respective provinces in order that hardships such as this may be obviated. It is obvious that a case of the kind is outside the principles which govern the dependents' allowance regulations.
I should like to say a word or two about dependents' allowances generally, and to draw to the attention of the minister what I think are anomalies in connection with their application. The principles which govern the granting of dependents' allowances are set out in regulation 98, and it is stated that a dependent's allowance may not be claimed as a right. As the minister has put it, the reason for the granting of dependents' allowances is to relieve the anxiety of soldiers who have enlisted. There is another principle involved in connection with the relationship of a man and a woman to which I think the dependents' allowance board should pay more attention.

War Appropriation-Army
I refer to possible legal rights as between the two parties. It seems to me that more attention should be paid to the actual legal rights of a woman. Let me give one case as an example. A man deserted his wife, ran away with another woman and set up a separate establishment. They were living in northern Saskatchewan under circumstances where he did not have any property. It was impossible for his wife to obtain a court order under the provincial jurisdiction. This man had lived with the other woman for three or four years. His legal wife was guiltless, but when her husband enlisted she was unable to get a dependent's allowance. The other woman, of the type commonly described as a common-law wife-I do not recognize the term-was able to get a dependent's allowance. It is true that some adjustment was made under which the soldier assigned a certain amount of his pay to his legal wife, but she could not get a dependent's allowance or anything like what she would have been entitled to if the soldier had not gone away with the other woman.
There are other similar cases. A wife may have a husband who is continually badgering her, and things reach the stage where he no longer contributes to her support. She finally loses her temper and puts him out of the house. He goes away and joins the army. Despite the fact that she has legal rights and could obtain a court order for maintenance, the dependents' allowance board still will not recognize her claim. It seems to me that in considering these cases the dependents' allowance board should depend more upon what are the legal rights of the wife. Like all other hon. members I have had considerable experience with individual cases. I believe the practice is to send an investigator, generally a member of a federal government department, into the community. He makes an investigation and presents a report upon which the dependents' allowance board makes its decision. This practice seems to me to be unfair. Because of an investigation carried on by one man, a woman may be deprived of her legal rights. If a woman is able to obtain a court order against a man, then she should be entitled to a dependent's allowance, and the report of a man appointed by the board to look into her case should be disregarded. The judge sitting on the case is in a position to hear the evidence and determine the rights as between parties.

Yes. Here is another one along the same line. A wife divorces her husband because he has committed some statutory offence which entitles her to a divorce. She is guiltless but just as soon as the decree nisi is granted the dependents' allowance board arbitrarily reduces her allowance, so that she is receiving less than she would be entitled to receive if she continued in her married state. This condition is brought about through no fault of her own. Her husband has been unfaithful, and the result is that she is left in a worse position than she was before. I suggest that that is an unfair position to put her in. A woman may not feel like going to court to obtain a divorce, because she knows that if she does, the amount she receives will be drastically reduced. The woman may be elderly and not able to earn anything; she may be depending entirely upon her legal rights in the civil courts, and yet the dependents' allowance board rules that she is entitled to considerably less than she would receive if she continued in her married state.
Could the minister give us some information as to the number of cases in which duplicate dependents' allowances have been paid?- that is, where a wife has been receiving more than one allowance because she is married to more than one man. There are one or two other points I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. I understand that this is a general item under which we can discuss matters which do not come specifically under other items.

speechtext:
I wish to express agreement to a certain extent with what I understand to be the principle enunciated by the last speaker. I believe it would be better for the dependents' allowance board to be given authority to pay attention to and be guided by

the rights of the wife, as between her and the husband. I realize the overriding principle in connection with these cases is that of freeing the soldier's mind from worry; but in the great majority of cases there is no violence done to that by recognizing also the rights of the wife with respect to the soldier. I am not suggesting that the dependents' allowance board give no attention to that, but I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the fact, as I believe it to be, that there is a tendency on the part of the dependents' allowance board to get away from recognizing the wife's rights as much as possible. I do not mean that it is done all the time. It has seemed to me in the last year and a half that in dealing with questions where there was something in the way of a dispute between husband and wife the dependents' allowance board was moving with much greater reluctance than seemed to be the case before. Of course I speak only from my own experience. It may not be in accord with the experience of other hon. members. I have seen a sense of tightening up on the part of the dependents' allowance board. I wish to draw to the attention of the committee two or three cases which have passed in front of me. I do so only for the purpose of citing them as typical of several. I am not interested in taking up the time of the committee with any particular case; I refer to it only as a type in order to illustrate the more or less mild complaint that I am making at the moment.
Before I mention the cases I wish to protect myself against you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee thinking that I am very critical of the dependents' allowance board and that I have had a bad experience with them. That is an impression I would not wish to convey because the contrary is the fact. I find in general that the dependents' allowance board are excellent people to get along with. They are doing an extremely fine job, but I think it would be a good thing if some directive could be given to them by the minister in connection with one or two matters.
May I illustrate the difficulty by giving the following case? A man and his wife got into trouble, the one with the other. They separated and had a case in court. The man was not working. There was no possibility of making an order against him for maintenance for the wife. The only thing the court could do in the circumstances was to give an order of separation and to give the custody of the child of the marriage to the wife. That having been accomplished, the husband departed from the neighbourhood for some little time at any rate. Later on he was found to be in the army. Of course, the wife always had the

War Appropriation-Army
right to apply for maintenance from this man, if, as and when she could catch up with him and he was in a position to maintain her. No order was given, for the simple reason that there was no use giving an order to get blood out of a stone. But when he is found in the army application is made for two things, the wife's maintenance and the child's maintenance. The dependents' allowance board follow the procedure whereby a soldier in such a case can be required to make an assignment. I think it is called D.A.B. form 14. This woman demonstrated the soundness of her position and the forms were filled in. This is many months ago. It was not a case where a wife sues her husband after he has enlisted and gets an order ex parte. They fought it out in court and she established her position. The procedure that was adopted was to endeavour to get the man to make an assignment, but he said he would not make an assignment. Apparently no further pressure was put on him, on behalf of the wife or the child, to make an assignment, except this. He said, "I will make an assignment in favour of the child if you put that child in such-and-such an institution". There the dependents' allowance board stood still. I am giving this as typical of some others, and I suggest that such a case requires some direction either from the minister in charge or from some other person on the government benches. I am quite sure of the facts. I am not stating anything hearsay; what I have said is absolutely correct. There is not the slightest variation from what is factual.

Another sort of difficulty I have come across from time to time involves also a domestic problem. A soldier marries a woman who already has one or two children by a former husband, or at any rate she has them whether by a former husband or not. It is perfectly clear that under provincial law that man marrying that woman with those children is responsible for the children of his wife just as he is responsible for the childen of himself and his wife. I find this curious development now, that although the soldier is admittedly liable for the upkeep of these children and is perfectly agreeable to maintaining them-whether he is agreeable or not he is liable at any rate -the board are now saying, "We won't give you dependents' allowance for the children of your wife unless you go through the procedure of adoption". Very often, and I think probably in the great majority of cases, the husband is quite agreeable to adopting the children, though I can conceive many instances in which the mother might not desire to have that done. But it does not make any difference whether or not one is agreeable; there is no reason why the dependents' allowance board should say, "We know you are liable for the maintenance of these children, but we will not grant any allowance for them unless you go through the courts in your province and become the foster father". That was not the situation formerly. I know of instances where it was suggested that the man should become the foster father-this was some three or four years ago-but he was told that he did not have to go through that procedure in order to have this allowance paid. I have come across two or three cases of that kind. Knowing what the practice was in the past, therefore I was greatly surprised recently to find that the board would not give these allowances unless the procedure I have mentioned was gone through, and I submit there is no reason why that should be the situation. I believe a directive should be given to the dependents' allowance board that in cases such as I have mentioned the allowance should be paid, so that the matter may be settled on proper legal grounds. There is no use in having one law with respect to liability while we follow a completely different course.

I realize that a blanket order cannot be made that the government will pay sufficient to maintain a home regardless of the income of the family, but where circumstances exist such as those I have described I think the board should be given some latitude.
Another matter to which I should like to. refer has to do with those cases where soldiers get into difficulties overseas. Under the regulations the allowance is paid for six months, and if a man gets into trouble with the military authorities he may be restored to his former status later on. I am referring particularly to the soldier in England who may have some difficulty with the civil authorities and receive a prison sentence of from eighteen months to two years.
In the case I have in mind the sentence was eighteen months. In this case the wife was notified that her allowance would be cut off at the end of six months, which would leave her without any allowance for a period of twelve months. I understand that a man such as this is automatically discharged from the service. That is not a nice prospect for a wife to face who has a family to take care of in Canada. She is to be put on her own resources after a certain period. If that man were in Canada there are ways and means of taking care of the woman and helping her out with her family obligations, but because the soldier is in England she is cut adrift without any assistance after the six months period. I do not think the wife and family in Canada should be forced to pay for any trouble the husband may get into in England. We have some responsibility for that family. I am not going to suggest what it should be-I have my own opinion-but I leave this with the minister, so that he may take it up with his officials and see if some relief cannot be given to families who find themselves in circumstances such as I have described.
The next matter I should like to deal with has to do with trades pay. I understand that 100-534
the regulations are not working as satisfactorily as we would like to have them work. Some of us who went through the last turmoil will remember that for twenty years we carried on a fight for tunnelers in particular in connection with trades pay. I have received several letters from men who were overseas and who claim that they have worked at occupations which entitled them to trades pay. They have returned to this country and have been discharged from the service, but up to date they have not received the trades pay which was promised them at the time. The same complaint is made by men serving in Canada. They say they have taken the necessary trades tests but that trades pay has not been paid as yet. I realize that this matter is pretty much in the hands of the commanding officer and that certain recommendations must be made by him, but there would appear to be considerable laxity.

The boy has made a good record in the service and has been promoted to a fairly high position. We do have to have regulations. We do have to have some principles laid down and some rules to guide the dependents' allowance board. The hon. member said that there should be some administrative latitude where there were extenuating circumstances. I have read some sections to-day which I think indicate pretty clearly that there is administrative latitude and in great degree. In extenuating circumstances the board has the discretion to give special consideration. In order further to extend those principles of equity we have established the dependents' board of trustees. This is another body which also has wide discretion in connection with cases considered to be meritorious. I should like to refer the committee to two sections in the dependents' allowance regulations which indicate the extent to which the board has discretion to exercise the administrative latitude to which my hon. friend refers. I refer first to proviso (vii) of article 101 on page 15 of the pamphlet, "Assigned Pay and Dependents' Allowance Regulations," which states:
In dealing with applications for allowances for "other dependents relatives", described in clauses (i), (ii), (iii) and (vi) of subparagraph
(c)	of this article . . .
Those clauses provide that "other dependent relatives" shall mean: (i) widowed mother or widowed foster mother; (ii) mother or foster mother whose husband has deserted her; (iii) mother or foster mother whose husband is alive but totally incapacitated; clauses (iv) and (v) refer to mother or foster mother having two, or three or more sons in the forces, and (vi) applies to father or foster father whose wife is dead. Proviso (vii) then continues:
. . . an allowance may be granted to such dependent relative provided that, in the opinion of the board, such relative is in a dependent condition and that the applicant has contributed wholly or to a substantial extent to the maintenance of such relative during a reasonable period of time immediately preceding enlistment; provided further that, even where the applicant has not actually so contributed, the board may in its discretion make a special allowance (not in any case, exceeding the maximum amount specified in subparagraph (e) of this article) in a ease where, in the opinion of
[Mr. Gillis.l
the board, the applicant would have so contributed but was prevented from doing so by circumstances beyond his control.
That is a fairly wide section to allow the board to take in dependents who are not included in the regular provisions of the act.
Let me refer now to article 119 of the regulations, which is even wider in scope and can be regarded as a superstructure built on all the regulations. It says:
Notwithstanding any provision of these regulations, whenever the board is of the opinion that a state of dependency exists-
A "state of dependency" does not mean only full dependency but also includes partial dependency:
-and that the granting of an allowance is in the public interest, but the board lacks authority to make an award, it may make a recommendation to the treasury board, and if that body concurs, the matter shall be decided by the governor in council, but no such grant by the overnor in council shall be construed as roadening the terms of these regulations. [DOT]
That is another article in the regulations, and in addition there is the dependents' board of trustees. So that I find it difficult to see how we can widen the terms of the regulations themselves and at the same time keep any principles on which all of us can work, least of all the board, if we go farther than the regulations which already confer so much discretionary power.
My hon. friend referred to one other matter, the question of mothers. I wish to make myself clear on this because my hon. friend took something that I said as indicating that the country would provide only the amount which the son had been contributing at the time he was supporting the parent. He said that I had said it was only a replacement of the son's contribution that the country was paying. I did not intend to convey that impression. It is not any replacement of the son's contribution so far as the amount goes. But the country does say, even if the son was not contributing at all to the parent's support, the question of an allowance may be given consideration. I want to point out that all that is required in order to qualify a widowed mother to receive a contribution from the board is to show that the officer or soldier was her sole or partial support. Even if he contributed only partially-I do not mean one dollar a month or something like that-the board may pay an allowance and need not limit its contribution, as I understand it, to the actual number of dollars which the mother lost by reason of the soldier going into the army. The board can say: We will pay in case of need up to $25 a month to the mother notwithstanding the fact that the son may

War Appropriation-Army
have contributed only five or ten dollars a month. 1 mention the point so that the committee will not get the idea that the allowance is just a meticulous replacement of the son's contribution and that nothing more can be provided. Whatever is granted must be within the limit set out in the regulations.
My hon. friend came back to the detention cases to which he referred the other night. I have every sympathy with the wife and with the children. I say to my hon. friend that he made a case the other night for this particular set of circumstances, but I do feel that he is not on very strong ground when we come to the matter of dependents' allowance. If the dependents' allowance is being paid in order that the man may be a good soldier, and the man is in detention and is not earning, then if the country pays the dependents' allowance for six months altogether, it seems to me that the country has contributed substantially toward the maintenance of the dependents and toward making whatever provision should be made for the wife and the children. My hon. friend was very careful in his suggestions. He did not say: I am suggesting a particular amount or a particular rule; but he did hope that the minister and his officials would take the matter into consideration to see if better provision could not be made than the provision which is here. I do want my hon. friend and the committee to bear in mind that we have to think of the good soldier too, as well as the soldier who is in detention for eighteen months and is going to be discharged afterwards. The good soldier stays on the job day in and day out; he does his training; he is ready to go overseas and get into the show; he makes his assigned pay, and he knows his wife receives dependents' allowance. It is not much of an inducement to keep him at his job to know that the other fellow who has deserved detention, who is absent without leave, or who has gone to gaol for eighteen months, is having dependents' allowance paid to his wife and children. One hon. member suggested the other night that in addition the country ought to pay the soldier's assigned pay which he would have assigned himself if he had stayed on the job, and that it should not be charged against him when he comes back to his regular duties. I suggest that is not quite a fair deal to the soldier who is trying to do his duty. I know it is tough on the wife and tough on the children, but at the same time a reasonable amount of consideration was shown them when six months provision was made. Nevertheless, as I said the other night, and I repeat, these matters are always open for consideration. This class of case, and the absent without leave case which
was brought up by my hon. friend and by some other hon. member, I am looking into and will keep before me.
My hon. friend also mentioned trades pay. I will look into cases of that kind at any time and keep on examining them. If a man has not received trades pay to which he is entitled, I am the last to say that that should be denied to him. Quite the reverse. I will try to see that payment is made if entitlement is shown.
Lastly, with regard to the sombre case of the casualty and parents having to make proof of death, if there is anything in that respect that can be done to speed things up, I assure my hon. friend that it will be done. I am cosntantly impressing that on my officers, not only with respect to the formal proof of death for purposes of insurance claims but also that all information with regard to casualties should be given just as speedily and as carefully and as sympathetically as it can possibly be given.

On February 15, at page 533 of Hansard I drew the minister's attention to the practice of the old age pensions branch in refusing a man old age pension because the wife was receiving dependents' allowance and assigned pay, in spite of the fact that the wife was investing the full amount of the assigned pay in victory bonds in the name of the soldier. I thought that where the total amount of the assigned pay is being held in trust for the soldier upon his return it should not be taken into consideration in figuring out the wife's income. If the assigned pay were not taken into consideration then the amount of the dependents' allowance itself would not in any way affect the full payment of the old age pension. I should like to draw the attention of the minister to a letter that was written by the deputy minister of pensions to Mr. MacFarlane, director of old age pensions. The letter is dated January 20, and in part reads as follows:
During the time the writer was chairman of the war veterans' allowance board we established the policy of exempting assigned pay where such was placed in trust for the return of the soldier or used to keep insurance in good standing or to meet taxes or payment on property owned by him. Where it is a veterans' allowance case and it was established to the satisfaction of the board that the moneys from the assigned pay were not being used for the maintenance of the parents of the soldier but kept in trust for the soldier himself, such sum would not be taken into consideration.
It does seem to me that the ruling of the war veterans' allowance board with regard to assigned pay invested in the name of the soldier is a good one. There is no 'reason why
War Appropriation-Army

a similar attitude could not be adopted by the old age pensions branch. I would suggest to the minister that perhaps he, in collaboration with the Minister of Pensions and National Health, get in touch with the Minister of Finance to see whether or not this matter could be reconsidered. When I brought this matter to the attention of the minister on February 15, he stated that he would reply on the following day. It no doubt skipped his memory on the following day and I did not have a chance to bring it to his attention.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer. Would the minister clarify the situation with regard to the rights of men receiving their discharge at their own request? As I understand the situation, a soldier receiving discharge at his own request does not receive the rehabilitation grants, namely, one month's pay and clothing allowance. This matter was discussed the other day, but I am still not clear with regard to it. I have three different classes in mind: first, the soldier who is brought back to Canada because his health has deteriorated and who has received a discharge at his own request. I understand that in that case he is eligible for the rehabilitation grant. Second, there is the case of a soldier overseas who receives his discharge on compassionate grounds. As an example let us assume that the father dies and the mother asks that the soldier be brought back in order to run the farm. I understand that in that case the rehabilitation grant is not paid. I have had two or three cases along that line referred to me. The third class refers to the soldier who has not gone overseas but who has had two or three years' service in Canada, and who applies for his discharge on compassionate grounds for reasons similar to the one I just mentioned. Would the minister clarify these three cases?	.
I should like to mention again the question of reductions from the dependents' allowance of dependents in T.B. sanatoria. The minister said the other night that he would be taking up that matter. I am wondering if he has had an opportunity to get any information in that connection. I received three more letters this morning regarding these cases. I hope I can get a reply that consideration has been given to them.
Before I sit down I should like again to mention the question of dependents' allowances, particularly the question of the assigned pay of soldiers serving sentence. I believe in a case where a man is serving a sentence and where the government have the man's body they should be able to get enough work out of him to continue dependents' allowance. If the minister feels that that cannot be done,
fMr. Quelch.]
at least the dependents' allowance ought to be continued and deducted from the man's pay after he has completed his sentence. I think the government should be able to do that in view of the fact that they have full control of the man, rather than to see the wife and the children penalized and put in a position where they have no money. In any event, the government could very well continue the allowance and take it out of the pay of the man when he has completed his sentence.

There are two matters about which I should like to ask the minister some questions. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Just before the committee rose for the dinner recess I had asked the minister why the government has not yet enacted a measure for Canada similar to the Sparkman act of the United States, under which men and women in the forces are protected in respect of their civil obligations. Then I went on to ask my second question, which was why Canada is not giving an adequate clothing allowance and rehabilitation grant to the men and women of the forces upon their discharge.

As I understand it, the clothing allowance was $35 until about December 1 last, when it was increased to $65. Surely the allowance should be large enough to accomplish its purpose, which I understand is to enable a man who has been discharged to outfit himself with civilian clothes. I do not suppose any hon. member will contend that $65 is sufficient for that purpose. It is not sufficient even in the balmy part of the country from which I come, out on the Pacific coast, let alone being sufficient back here in these arctic wastes. I find it very hard to understand why these young men and women are not given a proper clothing allowance.
The rehabilitation grant consists of one month's pay, together with whatever allowances the man was receiving at the time of his discharge. That, too, is insufficient. We must remember that many of these men have been in the forces for more than four years, and they should be given a grant large enough to afford them a reasonable chance to become reestablished. I know it may be said that provision is made for the training of these young men and women, that they may take certain courses and, while taking those courses, receive certain allowances. I do not wish to quarrel at all with the training provisions; I think they will be very beneficial, but the allowances paid during the training period are also ridiculously small. It may be contended also that these men can get unemployment insurance for a certain time if they are unemployed, "but I suggest to the minister that in the majority of cases our young men and women who are being and will be discharged from the forces merely want to get jobs, to get back to work. That will be the wish of the great majority, and I think they would ask for only a fair amount of help from the government. Probably they would believe that if they could get six months' pay, say, that would be fair. Perhaps not; they might want a greater amount. I see it was suggested by the national council of veterans' associations last December that the rehabilitation grant should be one month's pay and allowances for every six months of service, irrespective of the length of service.
The point I wish to make is that the grant should be such that these young men and women will feel that it is fair. Then their outlook will be friendly and cooperative. They are all good sports. If they received a fair grant, spent it as they saw fit and then, through any chance, failed to become reestablished, I do not think they would blame anyone but themselves. It is so important that these young men and women should believe and be

TFar Appropriation-Army
convinced that they are being treated fairly, and I do not think that is the situation at the present time. Certainly many of them believe that these allowances are not fair; that the government is chiselling, and so on. Not only do many of the men who are being discharged believe that; their friends believe it also, and I must admit that I do.
The outlook of these young men and women is vital to the future welfare of this nation. They are the most important portion 6f the Canadian population at the present time and will continue to be such after the war is over. I say that because of the sacrifices they are making, because they are young and fit and keen and disciplined and trained, and because leaving the forces they do so feeling proud of Canada, feeling proud that they have worn the name "Canada" on their shoulders. I believe the great majority of them have that idealism about their country which comes from serving it and being willing to make sacrifices for it. I believe further that they are prepared to take their full part in the life of the nation, asking and needing first of all only a little understanding on the part of the remainder of the Canadian people, and second, a fair chance to become reestablished. In many cases the effect of the smallness of these allowances, and also the inadequacy of our present pension law-which unfortunately I cannot discuss under this item-is to shatter their vision of a new Canada
That is a most unfortunate situation, and I suggest that the government and parliament must take the lead in remedying it. There is a great need right across Canada for an awakened and determined public opinion with regard to these young men and women. I am afraid that across the nation there is a great deal of indifference about what may happen to them, which reminds me of the indifference with which we all treated the young men who were picked up and sent to gaol during the depression days because they went around shaking tin cans, trying to get enough money to keep themselves alive. We did not like that; we felt that it offended our dignity a bit; but as a people, by and large, we did not rise in our wrath and say, "This thing has to stop. We are prepared to give up anything in order to see that these young men get enough to live on." We did not feel like that as a Canadian people, and I am afraid that as a Canadian people we are not feeling deeply enough now about seeing that these young men and women are properly resettled when they leave the forces. Everyone is busy; everyone is working; there is the excitement of war events every day; men who are being 100-54
discharged now are able to get temporary war jobs, and therefore the people do not see why they should bother.
I am afraid that is the general tendency, and I think it is a tragedy; I think it is something about which parliament should1 take some steps, for in my opinion parliament should give the lead. We need in Canada now-right now, not after the war, though we shall need it then as well-a determination to see to it that these young men and women are resettled no matter what the cost, and that they are given an opportunity to take a prominent part in the life of the nation. We have many problems in Canada to-day, and we shall have far more after the war. They will become increasingly serious, and ive need the help of these young men and women if we are to solve those problems. I believe our hopes for a better Canada are based almost entirely upon those young men and women who are now in our fighting forces.
And so I say, in summing up, that I do not consider these allowances or the present Canadian pension law fair to these young men and women. I believe that this committee, regardless of party lines, should insist upon fair treatment-in fact, upon generous treatment for these young folk, something that is more worthy of our country. If we will insist upon fair treatment I am convinced the people of Canada as a whole have only to be shown the need, and they will follow." They will make every necessary sacrifice in order to see that these young people get a proper start.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I shall not trouble the
committee by going into details in respect of the matters to which the hon. member has referred. He has really used, as the basis of his remarks, two measures, one of which he has said is the Sparkman act which, if I may put it this way, is not a major measure of rehabilitation or relief for ex-service men.
The remaining feature to which he has referred has been the matter of the clothing allowance given to the men on discharge. I share with my hon. friend-and he knows it, and I think the committee knows it, too-a full appreciation of the seriousness and the importance of looking after the men and women of our fighting forces. I can assure him that I am determined-and this is more than words-that every effort which can be put forward by the department over which I have the honour to preside shall be put forward.
First, of course, comes the winning of the war, as has been pointed out time and again. Second, and along with that, is the endeavour to ensure that we bring down and put into effect such measures as will make, not only

War Appropriation-Army

for the peace but for the happiness and security of the men and women who will have made victory possible. I say to my hon. friend when he asks for a lead in this regard- and I do not say it in any petty, party way, at all, nor do I suggest that he has done so- I agree that all of us have to be united in taking the lead in order to awaken this nation to the necessity for receiving these men and women some day, and helping to make Canada a country fit for heroes, both men and women, to live in.
I say to my hon. friend this, that we must put first things first. The first thing is to ensure that there is a post-war; that is to say, to ensure that there may be an end to the war, and to ensure that it is a successful conclusion. We are making every effort to make that just as sure as possible. When I made my short statement to the house I indicated the activities of the army in that respect, and I know my colleagues, the Minister of National Defence for Air, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, and other ministers who have to do with activities connected with the war will indicate what has been done in their departments to help to make victory certain.
But I wish to remind the committee anti my hon. friend that the government has not stopped there. I have said, and I repeat that sometimes I am concerned with the thought that perhaps there is too much talk and thinking about post-war, about rehabilitation, and about all the things which will come after the war when peace has been secured. We hear that talk when we have not yet reached our goal. At the same time I realize that, as is their right, people are thinking about these matters, and are looking forward to a future which will be brighter than the conditions we find to-night. I realize, too, that the men and women in our forces have similar thoughts. They are not professional soldiers; they are clerks: they are men from the farms; they are men from the factories and men from every other civilian occupation. They are Canadians who have turned aside from their real jobs, that of making Canada a great and prosperous country, to the job of making Canada free and secure. Those young people have a right to expect us to think of their welfare, and to endeavour to make plans for their future.
The government is trying to do that, and it has tried to give the lead to which my hon. friend has referred. That is mentioned in the speech from the throne, although it is not discussed in detail. There are a number of things to be done post-war, in the larger sphere, to which I shall not take the time to

refer this evening. It will be sufficient to mention them: the matter of export markets, the matter of world security and general prosperity.
After his excellency announced that "the winning of the war clearly remains the first of all objectives", we find these paragraphs in the speech from the throne:
Post-war planning falls naturally into three broad fields: preparation for the demobilization, rehabilitation and reestablishment in civil life of the men and women in the armed forces-
I say to my hon. friend that the government is trying to give a lead in that respect. I thank him for his support, and I believe the people of Canada generally will support that objective in every possible way. Then the paragraph continues:
-the reconversion of the economic life of the nation from a war-time to a peace-time basis, and its reconstruction in a manner which will, provide opportunities for useful employment for all who are willing and able to work-
Let me say to my hon. friend here that I believe I am speaking the mind of the men and women of our forces when I say that they are not as much concerned with the actual amount of a rehabilitation grant as they are with the question as to whether they will be able to find useful employment in this Canada of ours, and where they will get it. The paragraph continues:
-and the provision of insurance against major economic and social hazards.
Then, speaking particularly of the subject to which my hon. friend has referred, we find this paragraph:
A broad programme has already been developed for the reestablishment of veterans of the present war, and for the care of disabled veterans and the dependents of our fighting men and merchant seamen. You will be asked to approve a measure to provide w-ar service ratuities for all who have served in the armed orees, and also measures to supplement the existing rehabilitation programmes.
I refer to these matters because they cover the things to which the hon. member has referred. The matter of the Sparkman act, of which he has spoken, is one for the welfare of dependents. The matter of the clothing allowance given to men at the time of discharge is another matter of rehabilitation. The matter of one month's grant is still another rehabilitation matter. The objective is indicated by the programme I have read. It is indicated there that during this session the house "will be asked to approve a measure to provide war service gratuities for all who have served in the armed forces, and also measures to supplement the existing rehabilitation programme."

I am not saying that they will be what he considers sufficient, but I think he will find, when the house is asked to approve the measures which will be brought down, that they will meet the objective which we all have in mind, not only to recognize but to give assurance to the men and women who are fighting the battles of Canada to-day.
With respect to the Sparkman act, may I say that its principal feature is a provision of moratoria or of some sort of arrangement by which men who have insurance premiums to pay may not lose altogether the benefits of their policies in case they are not able to meet the premiums at the time they come due. A complete study has been made of this whole matter. There is one rather remarkable fact about the lapses in policies which have occurred during the years of war. According to the information we have, these lapses have been less proportionately for the men in the service than they have for the civilian population.

speechtext: There should not be any lapses.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will find that there has been very little request for this particular form of legislation. The situation when premiums are not paid is different in Canada from what it is in the United States. I understand that when a 100-54i
policy lapses in the United States they issue term insurance for the years or months which the cash surrender value of the policy would cover and that there is no provision for reinstatement. As my hon. friend knows, under our system the cash surrender value of a policy that lapses is devoted to the payment of premiums. So long as the cash surrender value lasts the policy is kept in good standing. Whether we should have had a Sparkman act or moratoria before is another matter. I have some opinion on that, but I think my hon. friend will find that the principle of the Sparkman act would be almost impossible of administration now. If policies have lapsed, they have lapsed, and there would seem to be almost insurmountable administrative difficulties in handling the situation in order to secure equitable treatment for holders of these lapsed policies, as well as equitable treatment for dependents.
I mention this to indicate to my hon. friend and the committee the serious doubt as to whether the principle of the Sparkman act would be workable in this country.
