I should like to bring one or two matters to the attention of the minister. because I think the debate has shown the need for them. I understand that the Whitelaw committee has recommended the doing away with, or has actually done away, with the office of the district welfare officers in the military districts. I think that was a very unwise move, because the district welfare officer is an officer given authority by the district officer commanding. His judgment carries a great deal more weight with the civilian authorities than does the opinion of the auxiliary services themselves. In view of the increasing number of cases that are brought to the attention of hon. members by sold'ers' dependents and by soldiers themselves. I think the district welfare officers should be reestablished. I anticipate that the difficulties will become worse as time goes on. I wish to make that point quite definite. This officer, who is responsible to the district officer commanding, has a very important function to perform.
The second point I wish to make is that a number of soldiers are at present classed as dese:1ers because they have been absent without leave, struck off strength, or lost to their unit

 sometimes for many, many months or even '-cars A case was brought to my atten-'
tion while my own unit was outside Liverpool during the bad blitz. Our headquarters was a transit depot. A number of troops were passing through, and when the blitz was on, these troops, who were not part of the unit, and not known personally to our officers except by name and number, went out and helped the civilian authorities and A.R.P. workers in putting out the fires and removing bomb damage. In Liverpool, and in a number of other cities, there are still air raid shelters and cellars where, because of the lack of workers, there are unidentified bodies which have been sealed in. I wish to ask the minister if anything has been done in that regard. We may have a soldier whom we now class as a deserter who may actually have been killed while engaged in the heroic duty of A.R.P. work during the bad blitzes. That situation was brought to my attention while I was in Liverpool. I do not know how many cases there are. I do not think there would be many, but I believe that there may be some soldiers who are now classed as deserters who may have died an heroic death.
I come back to the case of the soldier undergoing detention and having his dependents' allowance stopped. I do this because I have had some first-hand experience in the matter. While passing through the district depot at Aldershot I spent a day in the Aldershot military prison. I was in good company; I had a member of the cloth with me. This prison is used only for soldiers serving sentences of two years and upwards. I understand it is the supreme military prison in England. In a discussion of the matter with the commandant, the intelligence officer and the psychiatrist it was stated that our regulation was acting as a deterrent to making soldiers out of the Canadians in their custody. They pointed out that the families of the British, the Australians, the New Zealanders and the men of the Royal Marines received dependents' allowance, while our men were discriminated against, and our men were very bitter about it. Instead of accepting training willingly-and I may say that the prison was magnificently run and an excellent institution; it contained some of the most modern equipment and some of the most excellent training instructors I have ever seen were there-the Canadian soldiers in the prison were disgruntled and had a grievance. They were likely to try to escape. When they came out, instead of adopting the attitude, "I will never go back there again but try to become a good soldier," they had a grievance against the army generally and frequently were found to be repeaters. I believe that simply for the sake of the soldier himself and the psychologi-

War Appropriation-Army
cal reaction that he undergoes while serving a prison sentence, some thought should be given to this particular matter of dependents' allowance being paid on behalf of men undergoing detention. That is all I have to say about that particular question, but I think it is an angle that has not been emphasized sufficiently in this house.
When the United Kingdom soldier comes out he is smart and he is very likely to be noncommissioned officer material because the training is good, the rules in the prison are excellent and he receives intensive instruction; whereas when our man comes out he has a. grievance because of the discrepancy or differential in his treatment as compared with that of his brother in arms.
There is just one other point that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, and that concerns him jointly with the Minister of Pensions and National Health. It concerns the question of hospital allowances. When a soldier or an officer-and it is particularly hard on the officers-is discharged and is sent to hospital, when he is struck off strength he is put on hospital allowance, and the rates which I shall give to the committee constitute a great handicap to the officer undergoing hospital treatment. I am going to discuss an entirely different matter. This is about the only item under which an opportunity would be afforded to speak about this matter. I shall

War Appropriation-Army
be brief and explicit. I have not had an opportunity of taking it up with the minister's department, although I like to have a decision from that source before discussing any matter in the house.
The question I have in mind is one of discipline, and its application. I intend at some time in the future to go into this matter thoroughly with either the minister or his deputy. The fact is, however, that I happened to be in Camp Borden area yesterday morning and part of yesterday afternoon, and I had the privilege of sitting in on a magistrate's court. I was amazed to find that the Ontario provincial police had brought in a corporal from Camp Borden who was alleged to have committed an infraction of the regulations within the camp area. This corporal was in charge of one of the camp stores, and it was said that a revolver was missing. The provincial police were called in to make an investigation.
The point which arouses me is that that was an offence which took place within the precincts of the camp area. The boy was a clean-cut young fellow of about nineteen years of age and, in my opinion, instead of being taken to a civilian court by the civilian police, and instead of being placed in the hands of a rather tough crown prosecutor, without any representations being made from his unit, he should have been placed in a more favourable position. In this instance he had to hire the services of a civilian lawyer to defend him, and the amazing fact was that at least seven or eight members of his unit, headed by his company commander, and followed by his sergeant-major, his quartermaster-sergeant, and down to one of the troopers, took the stand and gave evidence against the boy. He was alone, with the exception of the civilian defence counsel he was obliged to hire.
The point is that if that young corporal is convicted in a civilian court and is sentenced to a term in a civilian gaol, he is a criminal and is automatically discharged from the army. He leaves the service with the record ol a convict. Having had some little experience in the service, and with an understanding of the experience the minister has had, I think he wall agree that if that is the esprit de corps being developed in that camp area-because I do not think it happens anywhere else in Canada-it does not speak very well for those who are in charge of that camp.
My question is this: Are the people responsible for discipline in that camp administering the policy of the minister's department with respect to an important matter of that kind? There is a lot more to this than what I have said. This is not the only case, but I have no
'Mr. Gillis.]
intention of delaying the committee, or of arguing the matter further. What I have said is based on what I saw myself, yesterday. In my opinion it is a most unfortunate mess. If it is not the policy of the department, then those who have placed the boy in that position should be called to account immediately. And if it is the policy of the department-and I do not believe it is-then I am sorry for the mothers and fathers of Canada who are placing boys of seventeen, eighteen and nineteen years of age under the control of people of that kind. Would the minister say if that is the policy of his department?

I do not think I propose to answer yes or no to the recital of facts regarding what the hon. member has said he saw, but with regard to which I have no information whatever. I cannot say what policy was being administered in connection with that matter until I have the full facts. From what my hon. friend has said, it would seem that the provincial police were seized of the case, for some reason which I do not know, but which may have been as a result of policy in that particular case.
I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend that a young man who is in the army should be defended in connection with a serious offence. But I do say that in connection with civilian offences, offences which are strictly civilian-and I say this straight from the shoulder-I have felt it was much better that civilian authorities should deal with such civilian offences, and that the army should deal with army offences. I have felt very often that discipline in the army to some extent has been rather flouted by the idea that we have had to have sometimes as many as seven men try a court martial, for weeks on end, on account of procedure which is laid down, and which has been in force so long that it is almost like the laws of the Medes and Persians. Then we might have an acquittal, and have the public wondering whether justice had been done, or whether something was being covered up.
With regard to civilian offences. I say to my hon. friend I have rather leaned toward the idea of having offences under the criminal code dealt with by the civilian authorities, even though committed by a soldier. On the other hand, with regard to army offences I have taken exactly the opposite position, because I consider offences such as neglect to the prejudice of good order and military discipline are matters which should properly be dealt with by army authorities.
In this instance I do not know what the case was about. From what the hon. member


War Appropriation-Army
said it would seem to me that this might have been a plain charge of theft; I do not know what else it could be. If it was theft, then I say to him that theft is a civilian offence. These arc cases which I believe the public will be better satisfied to have dealt with by civilian authorities. They are offences against the laws of the land, although committed by soldiers. Courts are set up for that purpose, and it seems to me that they could probably deal with such cases to better advantage. Then no suggestion could be made that the army is covering up something in connection with its own administration.
Before I could give my hon. friend a categorical reply as to whether or not that particular case represents the policy of the department, I would want to know all the facts, and the reasons for what took place. He can be sure of this, that I will know before this time to-morrow just what the circumstances were, and'be prepared to tell the committee about it.

I presume that this item gives me an opportunity to ask the question which I brought up some three weeks ago, with respect to which there has as yet been no answer. The question whether or not consideration has been given to the establishment of a rotating system of furloughs for our men overseas, so that after the expiry of a given period of active service they will be enabled to come home to their loved ones. In bringing this matter up I realize that difficulties would be encountered, but I do not
believe that they are insurmountable, A system of rotating furloughs is now being brought into effect in the United States. I think this is a matter that would do much to improve the morale of the men who serve in the army. In so far as those who serve in the air force are concerned, after a period of tour of duty an opportunity is given them to come home on furlough. The men who serve in the navy are given opportunities of furlough; after a period of service they are permitted to return home on furlough.
The system that has been considered over a period of time and is being adopted in the United States is one that is enabling men in the armed forces, particularly in the army, to return home. I think I can do no better than to quote from a periodical some of the provisions and the comments on the provisions that are made in respect thereto:
The military services are giving more and more attention to the problem of rotating men who have served long periods overseas. Plans already have been v'orked out by the war department to provide trips home and furloughs for men serving in certain areas, and consideration is being given to similiar rotation for men in some of the foreign theatres.
I point out that many of our men have spent five Christmases overseas.
A limited number of men in the North African theatre, who have eighteen months' foreign service behind them are being rotated home each month. The marine corps tries to bring home each month three per cent of its men serving overseas.
I realize there are difficulties. One of the difficulties would naturally be the question of reinforcements. We have the assurance of the minister, if I understood him correctly, that the necessary' reinforcements are available. Another difficulty would be the question of the necessary shipping. I do not think that is an insuperable difficulty any longer, having regard to the production of ships. Quite a number of the loved ones of these men who have been overseas for four and a half years have asked me whether it would be possible to bring into effect in Canada a system similar to that now being put into operation in the United States, to the end that men in the army shall receive a measure of the consideration in this regard as do those who serve in the navy and the air force. speechtext:
I understand that the care of those prisoners comes under the Depart-mcnt of National Defence. Could the minister tell us whether or not there has been any change in the handling of prisoners in view of the fact that so many of them are now allowed to work on farms? As I understand it, the discipline within camps is handled entirely by the nazis themselves; they have a little gestapo inside which handles all the occupants. I am just wondering whether there has been a change in the administration or in the sort of control that is exercised over the nazis in the camps.
fMr. Ralston.]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I want to say to my hon. friend that I do think the statement he makes is a bit ill-advised. I have not heard of the occurrences of which my hon. friend speaks. Within the last three weeks a representative of the protecting power has visited internment camps all over Canada. Of course he will make his report to the German government, and we endeavoured to show him everything there was to be seen. I have not heard of any such events as those to which my hon. friend refers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That has nothing to do with the guards; it is all within the camps.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, a certain number of these men are out on parole, and I think they have done very good work; but that is a comparatively small percentage of the number we have in camp. There has been no change in the camp organization to which he refers; and that organization, under which there are camp leaders, is the organization that has been adopted from the very beginning, the usual organization in connection with internment camps. In fact, I think it is by all means, so far as I can find out, the best way to run an internment camp, namely, to have the camp leader responsible to the camp commandant, or to his staff, for order and discipline among the men.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The German leader inside is responsible?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He is the one who represents the wishes, representations and complaints of his fellow prisoners of war. Everything to be brought to the attention of the camp officials is done through the camp leader. Generally he is the one who deals with the representative from the protecting power, when that official visits the camp to ascertain what the conditions are, in order that he may report to the German government. On the other hand, we also get a report from camps in Germany.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The German leader in the camp is responsible for the discipline?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would not say he is altogether responsible for the discipline, because he has not himself any power to enforce. However, he is the head of the organization in the camp, and the one who is regarded as the representative of the men. I suppose they have the same troubles as similarly organized democratic bodies have. Sometimes a leader does not always represent everybody in a camp. But it seems to me that this is eminently the most desirable and the best way to run these camps efficiently.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Although I am not going into details in the matter, I desire to ask certain questions with regard to one James Clark, a former chief inspector of the inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada, and allegations made by him, to which reference has been made in the press to the effect that in the supplying of shoes for the Canadian army materials were not in accordance with specifications, in connection with about a million pairs of boots, and that 30,000 pairs were made on lasts contrary to specifications.
My questions are these: Have these allegations by the former chief inspector been brought to the attention of the minister? What investigation has been made by him of the allegations made by Mr. Clark? Will the minister lay on the table the findings of any investigation that was made? Finally, what does the government intend to do toward having a judicial investigation into the allegations?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I cannot believe that my hon. friend really understands the genesis of this matter when I consider the questions he has asked.
Mr. DIEFENBAKER,: What does the min ister mean by the genesis?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The genesis of this inquiry. These allegations were made by a man who was dismissed last August. As I remember it, he started out with the allegation that he had discovered, I think in November, 1942, nine months before, that some other inspector had received a bottle of liquor as a present from one of the contractors, and he admitted that he himself had participated. Having been dismissed in August, 1943, Mr. Clark has several times since insisted that he be reinstated because, as he say's, that he was wrongly dismissed. He has accompanied that request with certain charges. In November or Decem-
(Mr. Ralston.]
ber, 1942, he alleged that there were irregularities on the part of other inspectors nine months; that was about nine months before he was dismissed. The allegations he made with regard to the boots were with regard to boots that had been inspected-I have not the dates before me-I believe in 1941 and 1942.
It is necessary for the committee to understand that the board for which Mr. Clark was working was the joint inspection board of Canada and the United Kingdom. That board was set up in 1940 under Major-General Sir Robert Lock, a British officer, and it has approximately 15,000 employees. It does the inspection in the United States of munitions and supplies purchased for the United Kingdom and Canada, and in Canada of munitions and supplies for Canada, China, Great Britain, Russia and other countries purchasing Canadian goods. It is a joint board which reports to the British government through the Right Hon. Malcolm MacDonald, the High Commissioner for Canada, and to the Canadian government through the Minister of National Defence. Neither the Minister of National Defence nor Mr. MacDonald have interfered in any way with the administration of that board. All wre have done is to follow the terms of the order in council with regard to salaries and appointments of employees and to see that the financial commitments were within the terms of the order.
I feel it is necessary to say this because my hon. friend has asked whether the minister made an investigation of these charges. I say at once that the minister did not make an investigation of these charges. The matter was referred to the board and the board made an investigation. I understand that Colonel Currie, my deputy minister, went into the matter again so far as the Canadian government was concerned, and the board later filed a categorical answer to each one of the allegations made by Mr. Clark.
When these charges were made, Mr. Clark felt that he had not received satisfaction from the minister, from the Department of National Defence or from the board, and he intimated that he was going to publish his charges. It was felt that it would be distinctly against the interest of our war activities if allegations of this kind were made, particularly in connection with boots, the quality of which I think has been par excellence so far as I can find out from the troops themselves. It was thought that possibly the publication of this article would be reconsidered when the report, of the board was received. Therefore Mr. MacDonald and I took the unusual course of furnishing such information as the board had at hand on

War Appropriation-Army
each of the points mentioned in the draft article submitted We did that instead of allowing the article to be published and the matter to be plunged into the maelstrom of controversy.
As I say, this board has some 15,000 employees and it inspects guns, Bren guns, tanks and all sorts of equipment purchased by the allied nations in Canada and the United States. To have a statement made by an employee of the board that there had been wrong inspection or something of that kind would undermine confidence, and it was felt that the examination which had been made indicated that publication perhaps would be unwarranted. At the same time as I have said, full information was given by the board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Who made the
examination?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The examination was made by the board, by Brigadier Howard, who is now chairman of the board since Major-General Lock has resigned, and his officials. The result was that a full statement was made with regard to these matters. I shall just give my hon. friend an answer to two of them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Was the reply published?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. The first thing my hon. friend mentioned was that about a million pairs of boots were made with inferior material.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I said that was the allegation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Clark's allegation was that about one million pairs of army boots had been made with ground cork mixed with resin used as a filler between the outer sole and the inner sole in place of tarred felt filler that had formerly been used. Then follows a statement in brackets:
(Mr. Clark explains that heat from summer pavements and the heat from the soldiers' feet combined with the weight of the body when walking caused this ground cork to creep into mounds as large as two fingers inside the boots.)
The answer was:
Tarred felt or leather filler was specified and supplied until May 28, 1940-
That is nearly four years ago.
-on which date specification was changed to ground cork and resins compound (as a filler between the middle and inner soles) as the felt was unobtainable -when stocks on band were exhausted. Furthermore, skilled workmen were not available to process the leather filler, which was not in general commercial use. On December 16, 1941, when tarred felt again became available, the specifications were changed back to tarred felt. After this change in specifications had been implemented no further boots were accepted with the cork and resins compound filler.
That is the first allegation my hon. friend has made. The answer, to make it short, was that because of a lack of materials the specification had to be changed in May, 1940. The changed specifications were in effect until December 16, 1941. After December 16, 1941, tarred felt again became available and the specifications were changed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not understand what the minister means when he says, "the first allegation my hon. friend has made". I said that that was the allegation made by Mr. Clark.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend has taken the responsibility for bringing it up in the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am asking what the government is going to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He has taken a serious responsibility. I was going to bring down the papers which have been asked for by my hon. friend, but he has seen fit to bring it up and he will have to have the statement; that is all. I do not propose to have anybody get the idea that there is anything wrong with the boots being inspected by the joint inspection board for Canada, which board has, I think, done as magnificent a job in the way of inspection of Canadian equipment as any institution anywhere in connection with this whole war. For my hon. friend to bring this up now, a two-year old complaint, made by a man dismissed in August, 1943, is for him to take quite a responsibility, and I do not blame him for trying to get out from under by saying that this is Mr. Clark's allegation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I only asked questions which the people of Canada have the right to have answered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They have been answered already in the newspapers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend does not answer them by not answering them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have answered them just as my hon. friend has asked them. My hon. friend is bringing into this house an allegation made by a dismissed employee of the board, dismissed last August, and this dismissed employee himself admits, in November, 1942, that he received presents of whiskey, an irregularity which he says occurred nine months before that. That is the man my hon. friend now cites as making these charges. I am pointing out that the first charge is just two years old now, and has to do with boots the last of which were supplied two years ago. I have given the statement which was given
War Appropriation-Army

me by the board and which I have verified through the Department of Munitions and Supply, that on account of lack of materials a change was made in the specifications. That is the million pairs of army boots as to which Mr. Clark, my hon. friend says, makes changes, but I say that my hon. friend is in effect making the charges himself and taking responsibility for them. According to the report of the board these million pairs of inferior boots were delivered according to specifications, the specifications having had to be changed because of a lack of material.
What was my hon. friend's other question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It had to do with thirty thousand pairs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The statement was:
More than thirty thousand pairs of army boots were made by one contractor on lasts contrary to the specifications. These lasts had hunks of leather called cheaters built on them to give the approximate measurements of the proper lasts. This practice, he says, is wrong and would produce ill-fitting boots, and is never adopted by manufacturers of good quality boots when proper fit and comfort are demanded. '
And this is the answer of the board to that:
One contractor was permitted by the inspection board to use so-called "increasers" for a period of approximately three months early in 1941 as a temporary expedient at a time of change-over in lasts because he could not obtain new lasts in time to meet urgent delivery requirements.
That charge is in regard to 1941, and my hon. friend knows it. He has read this statement, and yet he stands here to-night and makes himself the mouthpiece of Mr. Clark in connection with this charge. The board's answer continues:
During that period it is estimated that he produced on these altered lasts less than-
Howt many?

4,500 pairs of boots.
That was early in 1941.
. . . The fit of such boots was considered satisfactory by the inspection board.
There are the two charges to which my hon. friend has referred. The matter was brought to the attention of the department. As I say, the minister never investigated the charges. I have not time to investigate charges of that kind under those circumstances. I handed the matter over to the deputy minister; the deputy minister had the inspection board examine it, and there is the board's answer with regard to it. I say to my hon. friend that if he wants an investigation-I have consulted the Right Hon. Mr. MacDonald, the High Commissioner, and regrettable though it is that this matter should be brought up

under these circumstances and at this stage two or three years after the thing occurred,. Mr. MacDonald did concede that if my hon. friend wants any investigation he is welcome to it and we will see that the papers are furnished to the war expenditures committee or whoever is the proper authority to deal with it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have one complaint against this item. It is like a salad, made up of things that are not supposed to go together. There is first of all: Personnel supplies and services; then food, medical and dental stores; then clothing and personal equipment. There should be a separate item for each. We should know how much is to be spent for food, how much for medical stores, and how much for dental stores.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend was not in when I gave the break-down.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We should not have to ask for it in the house. It should appear in the estimates before us. It should not be necessary for the minister to put it on Hansard. The estimates should be complete in the first place. Moreover, I complain because the minister appears to think he is gracious to give us this information. We are entitled to it; we have a right to it. He is not doing a favour to any hon. member by giving the details. We have a right to get them at firsthand, in the estimates themselves. It should not be necessary to give them in the house. They should appear in the estimates, I repeat, as was done in the last war. Why has this change been made? The minister is responsible because he is perpetually the acting Minister of Finance. It is nothing to make a joke of, and if it is to be treated as a joke I will tell again the story of Barclay's bank-and even about the empty bottles of John de Kuyper "compound gin." All these items I have mentioned are mixed up together, instead of appearing separately in the estimates, and they are mixed up deliberately in order that members of parliament may remain in a fog.
I do not agree often with the hon. member for Lake Centre, although he is a friend of mine; but he was right, from the start, in bringing forward the case he did to-night. Every member who has asked for information was right. I do not agree with their political opinions; but if an hon. member is thirsting for information, he has a right to have his thirst quenched. It is not a matter for laughter; 'it is nothing funny. We are responsible to the electors of this country for the expenditure of this money. Moreover, we are responsible to the army for the expenditure of this money, in order that the army


War Appropriation-Army
may get the most benefit from it. That is my point. It is no joke; it is a very serious matter.
The other day I mentioned to the parliamentary assistant to the minister the case of a young man who suffered with heart trouble, and who asked for a doctor and was refused a doctor, and who died that night. Then there was a case at Barriefield, where soldiers do not have the proper care they are supposed to receive. How is it that members of parliament have to complain of these things? It is a real shame that they have to be aired in the House of Commons of Canada, when there should be no complaint at all about the medical services being provided for our army. When I complained about that last year I was jeered at by the minister, but afterwards I made my case and established clearly that I was not exaggerating. Here again I should like to praise the parliamentary assistant to the minister, and I give credit to the minister, too, for understanding afterwards that the case was serious and deserved special consideration. It is not fun for me to rise now and mention these things. There is no excuse for that in our country. Soldiers should not be dealt with by the medical corps as they have been. There have been numerous instances like those I have mentioned, and it is not only in the province of Quebec that they take place. It happens also in the Simon-pure province of Ontario.. You have only to go to Barriefield, and many other places to see that.
For the edification of my colleagues from other provinces I will say that in the province of Quebec we have at least fifteen non-Aryan doctors, some with names that are not even Jewish. There are some with names like Ashkezany, and other names I cannot spell. Where do they come from? They are not British. They are not French Canadian. Where do they come from? They are the doctors who examine our boys. There are at least fifteen non-Aryan, to use classical language. At least one-third of the doctors in the province of Quebec are English-speaking. When I complain that the boys have not been attended to as they should have been I put the blame on the organization as it is. It is impossible to get reforms in the province of Quebec unless the district medical officer there is fired. I have complained, but he is kept there by political strings. That is why there is no order in the medical corps in the district of Quebec.
I can speak about Montreal, too, and about the way young men are dealt with at Longueuil, how they were attended to by the non-Aryan doctors. I am thinking of a young man who suffered from a heart condition and
who was told to shovel stones in a cart for a whole day. I looked after him. I fought his case for a long time. The parliamentary assistant to the minister must remember the case. He helped me. I thank him for that, but I, as a member of parliament, should not have been forced to go to the parliamentary assistant to the minister to have that wrong redressed. It is a shame that I was forced to go there. The father and mother were so thankful that after the boy, who had a weak heart and could hardly walk, was discharged from the army, they told me that they had no objection at all to the boy staying in the army if he was well enough, if his health permitted it. But when a fellow is sick like that, why should he stay in the army? He should be discharged at once, if he were examined by competent doctors.
I am not exaggerating now, but the father and mother were so thankful that they motored from Montreal at six o'clock in the morning and came to see me at Riviere du Loup the same evening. They came there to thank me for what I had done. I had not done anything except brought to the attention of the department the incompetence of some doctor.
I have other cases. I recall a boy who was staying on the farm for some time due to some misunderstanding. He was brought to the camp, and this is what happened. He was confined to barracks as a deserter, condemned to ten or twelve months. I fought his case again, and successfully. They finally decided to free him, and after months and months they found that he was unfit. He should not have been called into the army. He should not have been put in the C.B. He was unfit. Why was he a prisoner, and why did he have the shame of a deserter on his brow? It was precisely on account of the incompetence of those doctors.
Not only that, but they are snobs. Why is it that dentists and doctors have commissions and druggists have not? The druggists are snubbed by the medical corps. They are not considered as doctors although they could kill the whole German army with poisons they could prepare, and they could cure lots of our boys by giving them the proper treatments. I bring this to the attention of the minister. I hope he will reconsider it. I hope he will realize that the druggists are suffering an injustice by not receiving the same commissions as the medical doctors, the dentists and the nurses in the army. The nurse is an officer. Why should not the druggist be an officer? He is a responsible man. When somebody prescribes without being qualified the consequences must be serious. These men are leaving a profession which is honourable
War Appropriation-Army

and which deserves the same credit as the medical profession. I do not see why they are snubbed, why they are given the cold shoulder in the army. Those who get easy promotions in the, army are those who are backed by powerful drug [DOT]companies. I do not know what strings they pull, but when they belong to some big drug-making organization then they are sure to be captainized and majorized, made captains and majors. Everybody knows about that. Is it fair for a man who has taken the same course of study, incurred the same expenses to be a dentist and who belongs to that honourable profession to be treated like that? I have sent letters to the parliamentary assistant to the minister from the president of the society of druggists in the province of Quebec. I hope that matter will be considered and that the letters will be answered in due course.
Now I shall scandalize you, Mr. Chairman. There is an item in the estimates for clothing. For several years while the present Minister of National War Services was deputy minister of the Department of National Defence and when his successor, a very good man, Colonel H. Desrosiers, was in office, I succeeded in getting some second-hand clothing, especially long coats that had been worn by the soldiers, for the poor and needy, and one year just before New Year's I obtained 300 coats like that which I divided in two. I gave 150 to the needy families at Riviere du Loup, one for each family. I then had bales made of the second group, and this second-hand clothing was sent to the settlements and distributed by the parish priest or the mayor to needy families whose children could not go out in the winter because they had no clothes. I paid the freight from Quebec or Ottawa to Riviere du Loup and from Riviere du Loup to the other places where it was distributed. That clothing was of no use to the Department of National Defence. It was worn, but it Was still good when it was tailored by the mothers for little children who are poor and could not go out in the winter, could not breathe fresh air, could not play in the snow. The present Minister of National War Services did it very well and so did the present deputy minister of National Defence. But finally I had a lot of difficulties on account of what had been decided by the war expenditures committee of the house. With all their learning the members of that committee decided, on the advice of some outsider, naturally an expert, that it was better to sell that kind of clothing; but there was an exception. The Indians have a right to it, but the whites cannot have it. It has gone to the

Indians because if they did not get that clothing the government would have to purchase some new clothing and give it to them. They are given the second-hand clothing. If it is good for the Indians, why is it impossible for the good, red-blooded Canadians to have it? There is something else. It is sold at 12i cents a pound to the Jews. I have been informed, and I wish to inform the minister, that some clothing has been sold to the Jews for 12^ cents a pound, some changes made and re-sold to the government afterwards as new. I do not say that as a definite matter, but I hope that the department will make an investigation into it.
I will go further than that. A friend of mine, who is the head of the colonization department in my county, wrote to someone who looks after the distribution of war material after the war and asked him if he would be given the same privilege as the Jew and if he could buy these clothes for 12i cents a pound to distribute to the needy settlers and the poor, and he was told that he could have an answer only after the war. Well, after the war the quantity of military clothing will naturally be much less. If Canada decides to occupy the whole of Europe then we may have some old clothes, but it will be pretty hard to bring them back here.
I hope that this matter will be considered. I do not believe in these pink soap-bubbles of future felicity. If we are to have a post-war that will not be worse than the present we must organize the present at once and realize that the health of little children, not only in the cities but also in the settlements and in any other part of the country, is most valuable and is a great national asset. What is the use of thinking of doctors and of remedies when the illness of the future can be prevented? Is it not better to prevent it than to cure it? The minister would be playing the role of Good Samaritan if he would see to it that this stupid recommendation of the war expenditures committee is overruled. I do not blame the members of the committee for that; they did not know. It was suggested to me that I should get in touch with all the members of the cabinet and I waited for a time to put the matter before the committee and to bring the committee to a consideration of brass tacks and the reality of facts.
This country will never be saved by dreams, however beautiful they may be. We must realize that there is poverty in our midst and that those who are poor deserve help. It is not a pleasure to go around the departments asking for old clothes; but when it helps even a few of our fellow citizens it is worth doing; and at the present time when wool is so scarce,

Radio Broadcasting Committee
when it is impossible to get good woollen clothing for the little ones, is it not reasonable to ask for the crumbs that fall from the table of the rich? Is it not reasonable to ask for the clothes that do not serve the army any longer, but which could very well serve another purpose for the betterment of living conditions in this country? _
It is a serious problem. It is not a problem of rags. It is a problem of giving the needy as much as possible under the hard circumstances we are going through, and I insist upon it. I am sure that what I have said has been a revelation to many hon. members who honour me by listening to what I am telling them. But there is no humiliation in speaking of these matters when good comes out of it. Is it not possible to come to an agreement about it?
I have no objection to the Indians having their share; they were the first citizens of the country. But when they get something I do not see why the whites cannot have it too. Moreover, let us not live in the future but in the present; and let us try to improve present conditions before discussing the future. The future will be what the present is. If the present is chaotic the future will be chaotic, and there will be no order in the future unless there is order now. But we can make the present orderly, provided we have no fancy schemes suggested by brilliant economists to make us forget what the present is. We must look the present in the face and try to do our bdst to remedy what is wrong by using sometimes the very simple means which are at our entire disposal. The only thing for the cabinet to do is to say yes; then to-morrow the matter will be settled for this year and for the year after, and every member will be in a position, if he needs it, to have some help for his constituency. This must not be neglected; it is important.
There is a lot I could say about the health of the boys in the army, and I am greatly surprised that it was left to a layman to speak about it. I waited for a long time because I expected some doctor to raise the point. I expected some doctor to explain how the pulhems system is working. It is a most absurd concoction from the British war office.

I will ask my hon. friend to keep quiet. It is a question of geography, and he is not interested in anything except the civil service and increases in salaries. I hope he will give me an opportunity to fight for my own people while he does his best to ' increase the salaries of the civil servants.
Progress reported.
